questions.text: How does call differ from apply?
options: call takes arguments one by one, apply takes an array. Both set this
apply sets this, call does not
call invokes the function, apply only binds this
No difference: both ignore the first argument

questions.text: Can call replace this on a function that was already bound?
options: Yes, the latest call always wins
Yes, if you pass the same object
No: bind already fixed this, and call does not change it

questions.text: Why do forEach and map take a second argument, thisArg?
options: It becomes this for an ordinary callback during the loop
It also replaces this for an arrow
It is the initial accumulator, as in reduce
It is the number of iterations

questions.text: What does new do with a function that was already bound?
options: new uses the bound object and does not create a new one
new ignores the bound this and creates a new object. Bound arguments stay
Such a function cannot be called with new
new drops both this and the bound arguments

questions.text: A second bind replaces the this fixed by the first bind.
call and apply can replace this on an arrow.
An ordinary class method pulled off an instance loses this.
A class arrow field remembers the instance even if the field is called on its own.
How does the const self = this trick work for a nested function?
questions.answer: self stores the method’s this in a variable. The inner function reads self from the closure, because its own this is no longer the object.

questions.text: Why does an arrow callback in forEach see the method’s this, while a plain function does not?
questions.answer: An arrow has no this of its own and takes the method’s. A plain function gets this from forEach: without thisArg that is undefined in strict mode.

questions.text: Where does a class method live, where does an arrow field live, and how does that affect this?
questions.answer: One method lives on the prototype, and this comes from the call. An arrow field is created on each instance and closes over that instance’s this.

questions.text: What remains of bind if the function is later called with new?
questions.answer: The bound this is dropped: new creates its own object. Arguments bound with bind are still prepended.
